items.abstract: <jats:p>The growing deployment of LLM-based autonomous agents has exposed a critical gap in evaluation methodology: existing benchmarks predominantly measure task success under nominal conditions, offering little insight into why agents fail or whether they can recover. This paper addresses the design of benchmarks and evaluation protocols that systematically diagnose agent failures and assess repair capabilities. We argue that meaningful robustness evaluation requires (i) controlled fault injection across architectural layers, (ii) fine-grained diagnosis localizing failures to specific components-input handling, prompting, tool use, or planning-and (iii) protocols that distinguish passive success from active recovery. Recent work has charted this territory with frameworks combining detection tools and rootcause analysis to uncover failures across agent layers, demonstrating that trace-grounded diagnosis substantially outperforms prompt-only repair strategies. Systematic perturbation taxonomies have been proposed-distinguishing transient from persistent faults and singlepath from multi-path tasks-with metrics quantifying recovery independent of task completion. Complementary evaluation frameworks have revealed significant reliability gaps between nominal and stressed performance across baseline architectures. Yet substantial challenges remain. Benchmark validity itself is a concern, with auditing pipelines detecting hidden flaws in widely used benchmarks, confounding model errors with benchmark artifacts. Diagnostic tools must bridge the gap between curated benchmark data and real LLM-generated traces, where feature-based detectors degrade considerably. Furthermore, the notion of "repair" requires operational definition-whether involving prompt refinement, tool schema updates, harness modification, or self-healing through closed-loop validation. This paper synthesizes these emerging threads to propose design principles for failure diagnosis and repair evaluation: composable fault scenarios targeting specific failure modes, multi-metric frameworks separating detection, localization, and repair effectiveness; regression-aware validation preventing repair-induced degradation; and architecture-agnostic protocols accommodating diverse assessment approaches. We discuss benchmark auditing as a prerequisite for trustworthy evaluation and outline open questions regarding generalization, calibration of LLM-based judges, and the transition from benchmark performance to deployment reliability.</jats:p>
title: Designing Benchmarks and Evaluation Protocols for Agent Failure Diagnosis and Repair Capabilities

items.abstract: <jats:p>Large Language Model (LLM) and Vision-Language Model (VLM) agents now execute API calls, construct database queries, browse dynamic web interfaces, and trigger backend transactions inside production software systems. Because the consequential output of such a system is an executed action rather than a paragraph, static text benchmarks such as HELM leave several failure modes unmeasured: demographic bias in discrete tool selection, unhandled runtime exceptions, corrupted transaction state, cascading multi-agent delusion, and a measurement artifact that inflates apparent bias whenever the fairness null is computed at the wrong group arity. This review synthesizes 59 sources into four governance pillars. Under action-space fairness auditing we set out the Bias Conduction Framework, Counterfactual Flip Rates, Mean Absolute Score Disparity, and the extreme-value expansion E[∆ K ] ≈ 2σ √ 2 ln K that AgentFairBench adopts as its null, and we show that this asymptotic form is loose at audit-scale group counts, deriving an exact arity mismatch factor of 2.25× for a six-group audit scored against a two-run baseline. Resource-efficient safety screening on commodity CPUs (TriEval) forms the second pillar. The third contrasts open-loop scaffolds such as ReAct and Toolformer against closed-loop architectures enforcing Abstract Syntax Tree schema validation, sandboxed execution, and transactional rollback (ExecuGraph), while the fourth covers predeployment governance through class-conditional Mondrian conformal calibration and multi-metric pre-clearance gating (RISED). Instability on the scoring side cuts across all four, since paraphrase-induced verdict flips in LLM-as-a-judge pipelines corrupt the statistics these audits consume. We establish a topological audit order, state the boundaries of the evidence base, and mark open IEEE research directions.</jats:p>
title: Autonomous Agent Reliability, Safety Auditing, and Action Fairness: A Systematic Review of Benchmarks, Execution Grounding, and Deployment Governance
